brief.head: Monks and tech bros
brief.text: Ajay Shah sees two strands in de­clut­ter­ing: the old ideal of the monk who owns noth­ing, and the tech bro pro­tect­ing his brain for in­tense work. {030-C02}

brief.head: Unread, not unwanted
brief.text: Amit Varma con­fesses to tsun­doku, own­ing more books than he reads. Unread books, he ar­gued, keep you sur­rounded by things you might yet dis­cover. {030-C07}

brief.head: Twelve shirts, no more
brief.text: The hosts’ friend Vishal Nevatia owns ex­actly twelve shirts. If a thir­teenth ar­rives, one must go, so junk can never pile up, Shah said. {030-C13}

brief.head: No to what you love
brief.text: Steve Jobs told Jony Ive to learn to say no to things he loved[[x6]], Amit Varma re­called. Saying no to what you dis­like is triv­ial. {030-C20}

brief.head: Pigsty superpower
brief.text: Needing a neat room be­fore you can think is a bur­den, Ajay Shah said. He trains him­self to work any­where, even at a rail­way sta­tion. {030-C16}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: How we live our days is how we live our lives.
thought.who: Annie Dillard’s line[[x7]], quoted by Amit Varma on living in the micro[[x8]]

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on things, minds and mess
lead.head: Less junk, more mess

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 30

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah recorded this episode out­doors, and Varma had an ex­pla­na­tion ready. “We are de­clut­ter­ing. We have done away with the house. We will not have a roof over our heads any­more. What a great life.” {030-J01}
The joke had a point. For Varma, de­clut­ter­ing is best summed up[[x1]] by the writer Chuck Palahniuk: the things you own end up own­ing you.
“If we carry too many things,” he said, “ev­ery­thing that we have lit­er­ally be­comes bag­gage for us.”
Both hosts ad­mit­ted to mixed feel­ings. So each set out the phi­los­o­phy he ac­tu­ally prac­tises.
## The junk in the head
Varma came to the sub­ject through his father’s death. Clearing his late father’s house[[x2]], full of books, trunks and cu­rios, he de­cided that his own mind had the same prob­lem.
The clut­ter that mat­ters most, he ar­gued, is men­tal: unim­por­tant pre­oc­cu­pa­tions crowd­ing out what mat­ters, and toxic, en­vi­ous or gos­sipy peo­ple who drain en­ergy. {030-C04}
His rem­edy is to live in the micro. Where he once wrote ten-item to-do lists and pan­icked, he now com­mits to one thing a day. Everything after that is a bonus.

Possessions worry him less. With his read­ing and writ­ing in the cloud, he en­joys things with­out being at­tached. “Every ma­te­rial thing that I have is re­place­able,” he said. “What is not re­place­able is time.”
Nor does he want life too tidy. Drawing on Tim Harford’s *Messy*, he warned that a life cu­rated into com­fort breeds au­topi­lot.
## A bunch of al­go­rithms
Shah de­scribed his own ap­proach as “a bunch of al­go­rithms”. Owning things, he said, puts a tax on the mind, so own­ing less is bet­ter.

India, he ar­gued, has an es­pe­cially big clut­ter prob­lem. Between about 1991 and 2011, trade bar­ri­ers fell and in­comes rose to­gether, and within twenty years the coun­try went from scarcity to plenty. Its thumb rules about what to buy and keep, he said, are now “a lit­tle off”. {030-C10}
His rules for buy­ing: ex­per­i­ment boldly with cheap gad­gets, since one good fit pays for many mis­takes, and never buy to im­press. Then be a “grim reaper” about what goes un­used.
Every fab­ri­cated ob­ject, Shah said, is a sta­tis­ti­cally im­prob­a­ble ar­range­ment of atoms, and de­serves to be used. If he is not using a thing, he gives it to some­one who will. {030-C14}
Varma’s caveat: by Sturgeon’s law most of what hu­mans make is crap, and he will not pass on a book he thinks is bad.
## The five and the fif­teen
The same think­ing ap­plied to peo­ple. Most of our emo­tional en­ergy, Shah said, cit­ing Robin Dunbar, goes to five peo­ple and then fif­teen more, so we should lav­ish our at­ten­tion on them.

With projects, he starts many and fin­ishes few, and calls this the in­no­va­tion fun­nel. “For each one line in the re­sume,” he said, “if you don’t have a hun­dred lines left be­hind, then you’re doing some­thing wrong.” {030-C18}
Varma, by his own ac­count an ex­pert pro­cras­ti­na­tor, saw a dan­ger: the fun­nel can be­come an ex­cuse never to ex­e­cute. He ar­gued for a bias to­wards ac­tion: pick any one idea and do it.

His clos­ing pick, Ken Liu’s *The Paper Menagerie*, was a les­son in de­clut­tered lan­guage, and he promised it would make Shah weep. “When we record our next episode, gen­tle reader,” he said, “Ajay’s eyes will be red.”

second.label: Toxic people
second.head: A part of me dies
second.deck: A friend’s confession in 1990s Bombay taught Amit Varma whom to keep away

pic.caption: Amit Varma on a friend’s envy

body: In the late 1990s, Amit Varma walked out of din­ner at Oh! Calcutta in Tardeo, Bombay, with a friend who is now a cel­e­brated and con­tro­ver­sial nov­el­ist. The friend said: “You know, Amit, every time a friend of mine does well, a part of me dies.” {030-S02}
He was only try­ing to be clever, but Varma stood in the street, stunned. Many peo­ple, he came to see, are like this: they smile and pre­tend to wish you well, but they don’t.

So he de­clut­ters peo­ple.[[x4]] He has cu­rated his Twitter feed to keep neg­a­tiv­ity out, and left WhatsApp groups where peo­ple gos­sip[[x3]] about oth­ers all day. {#twitter} “Why shit on oth­ers all the time?” he asked.

quote.text: You know, Amit, every time a friend of mine does well, a part of me dies.

third.head: The marathon that wasn’t
body: Ajay Shah wanted to know how Amit Varma ships an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* and one of *Everything is Everything* every week. Shah put his own share of the sec­ond at 30 per cent. {#thirtypercent}
“Badly,” Varma replied. The weekly dead­line[[x5]], he said, is what keeps the shows com­ing.

His 365 episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen* sound like a marathon, he said, but are re­ally 365 sprints. He does not sleep for two days be­fore a record­ing, then spends two days re­cov­er­ing. {030-S06}

His res­o­lu­tion for his “sec­ond half cen­tury” is a real marathon: an hour of writ­ing and two hours of read­ing every day. Explaining it, he mimed run­ning in his chair. “The rarest ob­ject in the world,” said Shah, “a Bengali sprinter.” {030-J11}

p2.title: The clutter question
p2.deck: Amit Varma tidies his mind, Ajay Shah runs algorithms for his things, and both make room for mess

quote.text: I will do one thing today. And once I have done that one thing, ev­ery­thing is a bonus, but I will chill.

box.title: The book that argues for mess
box.text: Tim Harford’s *Messy* makes the case that cre­ativ­ity comes from being pushed out of your com­fort zone. Amit Varma in­tro­duced the econ­o­mist and writer as “also a fel­low two-time win­ner of the Bastiat Prize”[[x9]]. {030-J18}

sections.label: A tidier mind
sections.head: A mind like his father’s house
sections.caption: clearing out his mind
body: Amit Varma ad­mits he is no ex­pert in min­i­mal­ism. He likes to col­lect things and owns thou­sands of books. Clearing his late father’s house in Chandigarh changed how he thought about it. {030-S01}

Nearly ev­ery­thing in that house was junk, he said, prob­a­bly even to his fa­ther. “But we ac­cu­mu­late, ac­cu­mu­late, ac­cu­mu­late.” His own mind, he re­alised, was the same: crowded with pre­oc­cu­pa­tions that kept him from the one or two things that re­ally mat­ter. {030-C04}
## How we live our days
He has been think­ing about the writer Annie Dillard’s line[[x10]]: “How we live our days is how we live our lives.” We fix on grand goals, he said, but life is an ac­cu­mu­la­tion of days. {030-J16}
So his res­o­lu­tion for 2024 is to live in the micro: one thing a day, then chill. On the day of record­ing, the one thing was shoot­ing three episodes. {030-C03}

Clearing the mind means clear­ing peo­ple too: those with neg­a­tive en­ergy, al­ways blam­ing oth­ers, en­ti­tled. Keep in­stead, he said, peo­ple who make you as­pire to be like some facet of them­selves.

~ Things are an­other mat­ter. If his lap­top conked off today, he would order an­other, since his data is in the cloud. Nor would he spurn things to live like a monk; there is, he said, “a cer­tain kind of false virtue” in that. {030-C05}

quote.text: I will do one thing today. And once I have done that one thing, ev­ery­thing is a bonus, but I will chill.

sections.label: The case for mess
sections.head: In praise of a little chaos
sections.caption: the uses of mess
body: Decluttering car­ries a dan­ger, Amit Varma ar­gued: a life cu­rated so tightly that ev­ery­thing sits in the com­fort zone, among fa­mil­iar voices one al­ready agrees with. {030-C06}
His ev­i­dence was the story that opens Tim Harford’s *Messy*. Keith Jarrett, handed a sub­stan­dard piano in Cologne, im­pro­vised a mas­ter­piece be­cause he could not play on au­topi­lot.

Varma craves rou­tine, be­cause he craves dis­ci­pline. But he also wants “that lit­tle bit of un­pre­dictabil­ity”. So he has promised the show’s col­lab­o­ra­tors, Nomsita and Vaishnav, to write by hand in a paper diary every day, be­cause on paper the mind works dif­fer­ently. {#diary}
## Many projects at once

Harford also cites the re­searchers Howard Gruber and Sara Davis, who found that cre­ative peo­ple often work on sev­eral projects at once, Darwin among them. Such peo­ple, in a phrase Varma learnt from Ajay Shah, are “above the API”. {030-J20}
Shah’s nephew Hemen, in a tiny New York flat, buys al­most noth­ing, be­cause space forces him to be in­ten­tional. Varma’s phrase for it, from the poet Ranjit Hoskote, was danc­ing in chains.

~ Varma him­self does not mind books piled on the floor. “I’m not gonna go all Marie Kondo,” he said. If things bring hap­pi­ness and don’t get in the way, he sees no prob­lem; the clut­ter that wor­ries him is men­tal. {030-J21}

quote.text: In a sense we are all danc­ing in chains. We have con­straints all around us, and we dance the best we can

sections.label: Rules for buying
sections.head: Many mistakes, one good watch
sections.caption: buying, boldly and selfishly
body: Owning things, Ajay Shah said, means car­ing for them, re­pair­ing them and pro­tect­ing them from de­pre­ci­a­tion, and all of it is a tax on the mind. So he would al­ways rather own less. {#taxonmind}

India’s prob­lem is acute. Since about 1991, trade bar­ri­ers fell and growth came to­gether, bring­ing “the won­ders of Amazon and AliExpress”. Habits built for scarcity, he ar­gued, now mis­judge what to buy and what to keep.
## The Casio div­i­dend

No re­view can tell you whether a gad­get fits your life; only try­ing it can. Shah’s favourite wrist­watch, a Casio, cost him about 1,100 ru­pees, and he went through many watches to find it. {#casio}

The gap be­tween that price and what he would hap­pily pay is con­sumer sur­plus, and it “pays for a lot of mis­takes”. So buy cheap gad­gets boldly, learn from them, and give away the misses. {030-C11}

Never buy to im­press, he said: “Be self­ish, live for your­self, and that’s a bet­ter life.” For clothes, start with cheap, func­tional ba­sics. Fashion is not all a con, and tech­ni­cal gear such as merino in­ners and hik­ing pants earns its place. {030-C12}
~ He also likes things that last. His body size has not changed since col­lege, he said, so he still wears pants that are thirty years old. {#pants}

quote.text: Gentle reader, that gap be­tween what you paid and what you’re will­ing to pay is called con­sumer sur­plus.

sections.label: Rules for giving
sections.head: Miracles in the cupboard
sections.caption: atoms, watches and the eye
body: As chil­dren grow, Ajay Shah said, they dis­cover the glory of bi­ol­ogy: every leaf, every fun­gus, every virus. Edward O. Wilson called this bio­philia. {030-R13}

Shah then turned to Richard Dawkins’s *The Blind Watchmaker*[[x11]]. {030-R14} A watch found on a beach im­plies a maker; the eye is just as im­prob­a­ble but has no de­signer. Shah flipped it around: the watch, too, is a sta­tis­ti­cally im­prob­a­ble group­ing of atoms, and some­thing mag­i­cal.
## The sunk cost of things

So he gives away what he does not use. {030-C14} What he paid is a sunk cost and ir­rel­e­vant. The only ques­tions are whether he uses a thing, and whether some­one else would. He dis­likes land­fills.
He buys gad­gets at two or five thou­sand ru­pees with­out notic­ing, ex­per­i­ments with them, reads the man­u­als, and passes on the ones that do not fit. {#price}
Amit Varma, re­minded of Bob Dylan’s *Every Grain of Sand*, shared Shah’s won­der at na­ture but not at all things human-made. By Sturgeon’s law, he said, 90 or 95 per cent of ev­ery­thing is crap.

~ Following Tyler Cowen, he will not gift a book he dis­likes, though pub­lish­ers send him many. “Why would I give them a bad book that they might read?” he asked, of read­ers who man­age one or two books a year. {030-C15}

quote.text: We are buy­ing mir­a­cles. If you take them back in a time ma­chine, each of these things is a mir­a­cle.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on atoms, watches and the eye

sections.label: People and projects
sections.head: Kiss a hundred frogs
sections.caption: the innovation funnel
body: Decluttering mat­ters most at “higher planes of ex­is­tence”, Ajay Shah said, be­cause the scarcest thing is our cog­ni­tive bur­den. He has trained him­self to work any­where, so that his think­ing needs no pre­con­di­tions. {030-C16}

People come next. Robin Dunbar found[[x12]] we can sus­tain about 150 mean­ing­ful con­nec­tions, with 40 per cent of our emo­tional en­ergy going to five peo­ple and 20 per cent to fif­teen more. {030-R15}
## The in­no­va­tion fun­nel

With projects, Shah no longer feels obliged to fin­ish what he starts. Like a sales fun­nel, he gen­er­ates many mad ideas, triages in­stinc­tively and car­ries few to com­ple­tion. Before you find your prince, he said, you have to kiss a hun­dred frogs. {030-J09}
He has 150 un­fin­ished pa­pers on his lap­top. {#papers} He picks one, blocks hours for it, works with full in­ten­sity while ig­nor­ing ev­ery­thing else, then comes out to triage again.

Amit Varma ad­mired the focus and re­called Steve Jobs telling Jony Ive to learn to say no to things you love. But the fun­nel, he warned, can be­come an ex­cuse for ex­pert pro­cras­ti­na­tors like him­self.
~ “It doesn’t mat­ter which of those hun­dred ideas you take up,” Varma said, “but frickin’ hell take up some­thing and do it.” {030-C21}

quote.text: But for each one line in the re­sume, if you don’t have a hun­dred lines left be­hind, then you’re doing some­thing wrong.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the innovation funnel

quote.text: We should just ac­cept that we are with our five fif­teen peo­ple, and we are going to lav­ish our lives and our at­ten­tion on them and that’s all there is and there will be noth­ing more

p3.title: Tales from the clear-out
p3.deck: A house, a piano, a village and a flat: the stories behind the ideas

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on clearing his late father’s home in Chandigarh
stories.head: Half a room in a big bungalow
body: Amit Varma’s fa­ther died dur­ing the sec­ond wave of Covid[[x14]]. He had been a re­tired IAS of­fi­cer, liv­ing in a huge bun­ga­low in Chandigarh, and some­one had to clear it.
The house was full: thou­sands of books, trunks, fur­ni­ture, all kinds of cu­rios. Despite all those rooms, Varma said, his fa­ther had ba­si­cally been liv­ing in half a room. {#halfroom}

Varma had no space in his own house for the books. So he brought three friends and told them to pick what­ever they wanted. His own rule was to keep only books he wanted to read that were so rare he could not get them any­where, not even as a down­load­able PDF. The rest went.

There was one ex­cep­tion. For ten years his fa­ther had urged him to take his fifty-volume set of the *Great Books of the Western World*[[x13]], and for ten years Varma had re­fused: in a Bombay apart­ment, the real es­tate would cost more than the books.
After his fa­ther died, he kept it. When he moved house re­cently, he gave away hun­dreds of books but took the set with him. “I’ll never read it,” he said. It is there for sen­ti­ment. {030-R21}
What struck him was that most of what filled the house was junk, prob­a­bly even to his fa­ther for most of his life. Then he looked at his own life.
~ “My own mind is like my father’s house,” he said. “It is full of junk, it is full of ac­cu­mu­lated crap and it gets in the way.” {030-S01}
stories.why: Clearing the house be­came a mir­ror. Years of ac­cu­mu­lated pre­oc­cu­pa­tions, Varma re­alised, were tak­ing up real es­tate in his mind that should go to what mat­ters, and a phys­i­cal clear-out turned into a men­tal one.
stories.postscript: Varma does most of his read­ing on Kindle. The fifty vol­umes, he ad­mits, are an arte­fact.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his father’s house

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a concert that nearly did not happen
stories.head: A broken piano’s finest hour
body: In Cologne in January 1975, Amit Varma said, a 17-year-old named Vera Brandes, the youngest con­cert or­gan­iser in Europe, had booked the leg­endary pi­anist Keith Jarrett. The show was sold out.

The hall could not get the piano Jarrett needed and sup­plied a mini ver­sion, “like a half piano”. Its sound did not reach the bal­cony and some keys did not work. It was pour­ing, so no re­place­ment could be brought, and Jarrett sat in his car, ready to leave.
Brandes knocked on his win­dow in tears. He agreed to play, for her. Hitting the keys harder[[x15]], work­ing within a nar­rower range on an in­stru­ment he had never played, he im­pro­vised.
~ The album sold three and a half mil­lion copies, the largest-selling solo jazz album ever, Varma said, if he re­mem­bered cor­rectly. {#cologne}
stories.why: Harford’s the­sis, as Varma told it: thrown out of his com­fort zone, Jarrett could not coast on au­topi­lot, and ge­nius fol­lowed. {030-S03} A life cu­rated into per­fect com­fort risks los­ing ex­actly that. {030-C06}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Cologne concert

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a novel, a question and the meaning of home
stories.head: Facing Mecca, thinking of home
body: On *The Seen and the Unseen*, the writer Amitava Kumar once told Amit Varma about a scene in Rahi Masoom Raza’s novel *Aadha Gaon*, set at the time of Partition.
Activists urge a Muslim vil­lager to go to Pakistan. When he prays, he replies, he turns to­wards Mecca; when he thinks of home, he thinks of his vil­lage, Gangauli.
Varma now asks guests: where is your Gangauli? Max Rodenbeck, who grew up in Cairo, said his is the Cairo of his child­hood, which no longer ex­ists. {030-S05}

~ Varma has no an­swer of his own. Cosmopolitan but not rooted, he lo­cates home in what­ever sur­rounds him: his books, his room, the vibe. Marvin Gaye’s *Wherever I Lay My Hat* comes close. “Except that when­ever I’ve had a hat, I’ve lost it,” he said. {030-J06}

quote.text: It is a Cairo of my child­hood. It no longer ex­ists.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Gangauli and home

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on his nephew’s very small New York flat
stories.head: Small flat, big discipline
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah both live in tiny houses in Bombay. Shah’s nephew Hemen has a very small flat in New York, and it has driven him to ex­tremes of de­clut­ter­ing.
Hemen thinks very hard be­fore buy­ing any­thing. By de­fault he does not own things; he buys only what re­ally fits his life and his tiny “bud­get con­straint of space”. {030-S04}
Shah added a jab. When peo­ple de­bate a min­i­mum size for af­ford­able hous­ing for the poor, he said, “I’d like to say go visit New York some­time.”
~ Varma saw Hemen as danc­ing in chains, the phrase he had from the poet Ranjit Hoskote. We all live within con­straints, and Hemen’s chains are space. {030-C08}

quote.text: So the short­age of space has driven him to be more in­ten­tional around ac­quir­ing things.

quiz.a: Three each: one on day one, two on day two, and so on.

quiz.a: Consumer sur­plus: the gap be­tween what he paid and would hap­pily pay.

quiz.a: Sturgeon’s law, which says ninety or ninety-five per cent of ev­ery­thing is crap.

quiz.a: First triage to choose one thing, then a block of hours at full in­ten­sity.

quiz.a: Cairo, but the Cairo of his child­hood, which he says no longer ex­ists.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 30. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Keith Jarrett (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Tim Harford (PopTech, CC BY-SA 2.0); Richard Dawkins (David Shankbone, CC BY 3.0); Edward O. Wilson (Jim Harrison, CC BY 2.5); Erich Fromm (Müller-May, CC BY-SA 3.0 de); Ken Liu (Larry D. Moore, CC BY 4.0); Bob Dylan (Raph_PH, CC BY 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.title: To Have or To Be?
shelf.creator: Erich Fromm
shelf.why: Fromm’s 1976 book was a pi­o­neer on these ques­tions: how to move be­yond the sim­ple con­sumerism many Indians dis­cov­ered only in the last 20–30 years, to­wards a bet­ter sense of why we are here and what gives life mean­ing.

shelf.title: The Paper Menagerie and Other Stories
shelf.creator: Ken Liu
shelf.why: Ken Liu’s col­lec­tion, whose title story Amit calls a mas­ter­piece of ‘de­clut­tered language’ (noth­ing in it doesn’t be­long) that will leave you weep­ing; he sends it to his writ­ing stu­dents, and the rest moved him to tears at in­di­vid­ual sen­tences.

shelf.why: It makes the case for em­brac­ing mess.

shelf.why: A cel­e­brated mas­ter­piece im­pro­vised on a sub­stan­dard piano Jarrett had never played.

shelf.title: Aadha Gaon
shelf.creator: Rahi Masoom Raza
shelf.why: A villager’s an­swer — Mecca for prayer, his vil­lage for home — cap­tures root­ed­ness and be­long­ing in a sin­gle line.

shelf.title: Ranjit Hoskote is Dancing in Chains (Episode 363, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The poet Ranjit Hoskote gave Amit the phrase ‘danc­ing in chains’: we all live within con­straints and dance as best we can.

shelf.title: Amitava Kumar Finds the Breath of Life (Episode 265, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The ori­gin of Amit’s re­cur­ring ‘Where is your Gangauli?’ ques­tion about home.

shelf.title: From Cairo to Delhi With Max Rodenbeck (Episode 281, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Rodenbeck’s an­swer, that his home is the Cairo of his child­hood which no longer ex­ists, is a poignant take on home as a van­ished place.

shelf.title: The Rooted Cosmopolitanism of Sugata Srinivasaraju (Episode 277, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Five and a half hours on Sugata Srinivasaraju’s life, the mi­lieu he grew up in and how he watched his city trans­form, of­fer­ing an ideal Amit calls ‘a treasure’: being both rooted and cos­mopoli­tan.

shelf.title: Varun Grover Is in the House (Episode 292, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s con­ver­sa­tion with Varun Grover, who shares his idea of home as what­ever sur­rounds you wher­ever you are com­fort­able: your books, your room, the vibe.

shelf.title: Wherever I Lay My Hat (That’s My Home)
shelf.creator: Marvin Gaye
shelf.why: A song Amit calls a mas­ter­piece, es­pe­cially in Paul Young’s cover, which cap­tures his idea of a por­ta­ble home you carry with you (though he has lost every hat he’s owned).

shelf.title: Every Grain of Sand
shelf.creator: Bob Dylan
shelf.why: A beau­ti­ful Dylan lyric about our place in the nat­u­ral order, ‘like every spar­row fall­ing, like every grain of sand’, which Amit uses for the idea that the an­swers are dis­trib­uted all around us.

shelf.title: Biophilia
shelf.creator: Edward O. Wilson
shelf.why: E.O.

shelf.title: The Blind Watchmaker
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins shows how in­tri­cate de­sign, like the eye, arises with­out a de­signer: the bi­o­log­i­cal coun­ter­part of Hayek’s point about economies.

shelf.title: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
shelf.creator: Robin Dunbar
shelf.why: Dunbar’s find­ing that we can sus­tain only about 150 mean­ing­ful re­la­tion­ships, in tiers of roughly 5, 15, 50 and 150, with most of our emo­tional en­ergy going to the clos­est few.

shelf.title: Time
shelf.creator: Pink Floyd
shelf.why: The line ‘plans that ei­ther come to naught or half a page of scrib­bled lines’ sums up his Zen at­ti­tude to­wards aban­doned work.

shelf.title: The Question That Steve Jobs Used to Ask Jony Ive Every Day
shelf.why: Source of the les­son to ‘learn to say no to things that you love’, which is the real dis­ci­pline of focus.

shelf.title: The Minimalists and The Minimalism Game
shelf.creator: Joshua Fields Millburn
shelf.why: Millburn’s idea that a happy life comes from sub­tract­ing, not adding.

shelf.title: AliExpress
shelf.why: ‘Gentle reader, if you have not used AliExpress, you should.’ It is part of the cheap bounty that makes ex­per­i­ment­ing with gad­gets af­ford­able.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

shelf.title: Great Books of the Western World
shelf.why: Mortimer Adler’s set, whose the­matic es­says on death, love, de­sire, pur­pose and agency draw on the en­tire canon, fill Amit with awe and send him to the orig­i­nal au­thors.

shelf.title: Magic Fruit: A Poetic Trip
shelf.creator: Vaishnav Vyas
shelf.why: A mu­si­cal play and po­etry by Vaishnav Vyas, one of the show’s young crew, which ‘ab­so­lutely blew [Amit] away’ with its cre­ativ­ity and am­bi­tion; he says it proves the young can have both youth and wis­dom.

laughs.text: Opening shot out­doors (chap­ter title: ‘Just the Tree of Us’). Amit: ‘It is be­cause we are de­clut­ter­ing. We have done away with the house. We will not have a roof over our heads any­more. What a great life.’

Amit on monk­ish re­nun­ci­a­tion: when monks preached a sparse life, ‘they did not have a Kindle. They did not have a Fender Strat. Easy for them to say. They per­haps did not even have air con­di­tion­ing. So what is there to lose?’
Ajay of­fers the min­i­mal­ist motto ‘He who dies with the least toys wins.’ Amit adds: ‘but it also mat­ters where you start.’
Amit on Harford’s book: ‘Messy, by the way, is M-E-S-S-Y, not the foot­baller.’
Amit cit­ing Marvin Gaye’s ‘Wherever I Lay My Hat, that’s my home’: ‘Except that when­ever I’ve had a hat, I’ve lost it. Which is pro­found.’
Amit in­ter­rupts Ajay’s ac­count of 1991-era scarcity: one thing that was abun­dant then but scarce now is ‘the days of our youth.’ The joke has to be ex­plained: ‘Our youth. We have grown older.’
Ajay: ‘be­fore you find your prince, you’ve got to kiss a hun­dred frogs.’ Amit: ‘Why you gig­gle like that? Have you ever kissed a frog?’
Amit mimes run­ning in his chair (‘this is very Bengali of me’). Ajay: ‘The rarest ob­ject in the world, a Bengali sprinter.’ Amit: ‘Extremely rare.’

Amit’s Erich Fromm joke: Fromm meets a ro­tund Bengali in a Kolkata mar­ket (Bengalis like talk­ing to for­eign­ers, ‘it makes them feel sophisticated’) and asks where he is from. ‘Eric Fromm.’ ‘No, that’s what I’m ask­ing — Eric from?’ Then: ‘Okay I’m sorry, I de­stroyed your rec­om­men­da­tion. Please buy the book now.’
Chuck Palahniuk’s ‘the things you own end up own­ing you’, Amit’s the­sis for the episode.
Annie Dillard: ‘How we live our days is how we live our lives.’
Amit: ‘I’m not gonna go all Marie Kondo and say, no, only have thirty things.’
Bob Dylan, ‘Every Grain of Sand’, read aloud by Amit: ‘I am hang­ing in the bal­ance of a per­fect fin­ished plan, like every spar­row fall­ing, like every grain of sand.’

Pink Floyd’s ‘Time’ from Dark Side of the Moon: ‘plans that ei­ther come to naught or half a page of scrib­bled lines.’ Ajay: ‘I have lots and lots of half page of scrib­bled lines and I’m okay, I’m all Zen with this.’
